meta: Venus, Cupid and Ceres, a newly discovered painting by Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem of 1604, on the saying that love grows cold without food and wine.
about: Venus, the goddess of love, is joined by Cupid and Ceres, goddess of grain, and grapes stand in for Bacchus, god of wine. The picture illustrates an old witticism, that without food and drink love grows cold. It is a newly discovered work by Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem. The museum points to the soft, translucent flesh as a sign of the naturalism that grew in northern Europe around 1600, when artists worked more and more from life, from models.

meta: Elegant people make music and flirt in a landscape in Jean Baptiste François Pater's fête galante of about 1730.
about: A fashionable party amuses itself in a landscape with music and flirting. At the left a woman holds a guitar and another a music book, and at the right a girl plays with a dog. Jean Baptiste François Pater painted the fête galante around 1730, and the Rijksmuseum holds it.

meta: A conservation case: how restorers rebuilt the lace collar and necklace in Jan Anthonisz. van Ravesteyn's Portrait of a Woman, 1620s.
about: The museum uses this portrait to show how a damaged painting is conserved. After earlier restorations were removed and the picture was cleaned, parts of the sitter's lace collar and elaborate necklace were missing. The conservator rebuilt them after studying the artist's technique in other works and copying his treatment of the surviving lace and the twisting necklace. A probable ornament at the back of the sitter's head was left blank, because there was not enough evidence to restore it without guessing.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Wade

meta: Mademoiselle Noblet in a large hat trimmed with bird-of-paradise plumes, a lithograph by Henri Grevedon.
about: A woman faces us in a three-quarter-length portrait, turned slightly to the right, in a large draped hat trimmed with bird-of-paradise plumes. The caption says she is Mademoiselle Noblet, lithographed from life by H. Grevedon. The print dates from around 1820.

meta: Fernand Cormon's Young African Woman, painted in Tunisia and renamed for the 2019 Musée d'Orsay show on Black models.
about: Fernand Cormon painted this picture during a stay in Tunisia, and it is now in the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Pau. It used to be called Young Negress, but it was renamed for the Musée d'Orsay exhibition Le Modèle noir, de Géricault à Matisse in 2019, to remove the racist connotations. Cormon was an orientalist painter who also painted factory interiors and prehistoric scenes. His Paris studio was thought one of the best, and his students included Matisse, Toulouse-Lautrec and Van Gogh.

meta: An embroiderer's workshop and tools in a plate of the Encyclopédie by Benoît-Louis Prévost, about 1760.
about: The plate is divided into two parts. At the top two women work in a room, one weaving at a loom and looking out at us and the other sitting at a table studying fabric patterns. Below are tools and embroidery patterns, labeled with figure numbers. Benoît-Louis Prévost made the plate around 1760 for the Encyclopedia.

meta: Four soldiers in a guardroom, one writing a letter, a dog on a mat, painted by Herman Frederik Carel ten Kate in 1865.
about: Four soldiers sit at tables in front of a hearth in a guardroom. One at the left writes a letter. Pieces of armor and a drum lie on the floor, and a dog lies on a mat in the foreground. A map on rollers hangs on the back wall at the right, and a coat of arms with an eagle is above the chimney. Herman Frederik Carel ten Kate painted it in 1865.

meta: A painted oval ceiling with Apollo and the Muses in the sky, a project by Jean Baptiste Marie Pierre, about 1760.
about: This project shows an oval ceiling without the room around it. At the center is a view of the sky past an oval entablature, with Apollo, the Muses and genii in it. The entablature rests on arches through which more structures can be seen, and in four of the arches pedestals stand with griffins crouching beside a clock-like form. Jean Baptiste Marie Pierre made it around 1760.

meta: Vulcan catches Mars and Venus in his invisible bronze net in Joachim Wtewael's small copper painting of 1604 to 1608.
about: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, the blacksmith Vulcan surprises his wife Venus with Mars. He forged an invisible bronze net and hid it on Mars's bed. Here Vulcan stands on Mars's discarded armor at the right while Cupid and Apollo hover above, pulling back the green canopy to show the astonished lovers. Other gods gather to watch and mock them, and in a scene beyond the bed Vulcan hammers out his net at the forge. Joachim Wtewael painted it on a small copper panel.

meta: Eberhard, Duke of Württemberg, kneels as a pilgrim before Jerusalem in Nicaise De Keyser's portrait of 1846.
about: Duke Eberhard of Württemberg kneels in armor with his arms crossed on his chest, a sword in his right hand and his eyes turned upward. The city of Jerusalem lies in the distance, since he is shown as a pilgrim in the Holy Land. Nicaise De Keyser painted the portrait in 1846, and the Rijksmuseum holds it.

meta: An Italian mountain landscape with a waterfall and a herdsman on a steep path, painted by Adam Pijnacker in 1649.
about: This is an Italian mountain landscape with a waterfall. At the upper right a herdsman with cattle walks along a steep path on the slope. Adam Pijnacker painted it in 1649, and the Rijksmuseum holds it.

meta: Félix Vallotton's The Red Room, Etretat of 1899, built from blocks of solid color like his woodcuts.
about: Vallotton worked from a personal photograph and focused on the daily life of his household. He used bold blocks of flat color, such as the red of the bed and the pink of a child's dress. The museum says the result has the graphic simplicity of his woodblock prints of interiors from the same years.

meta: Peasants harvest and eat in Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Harvesters of 1565, one of a cycle of the seasons.
about: Peasants harvest wheat while others eat, and a woman sits upright eating bread and cheese with pears on a white cloth in front of her. Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it in 1565 for the Antwerp banker Nicolaes Jonghelinck, one of a cycle of six pictures of the seasons. Wikipedia lists many activities of 16th-century rural life, among them a figure picking pears and villagers playing cock throwing. The Metropolitan Museum calls it a watershed in Western art and the first modern landscape.
dimensions: Overall, including added strips at top, bottom, and right, 46 7/8 x 63 3/4 in. (119 x 162 cm); original painted surface 45 7/8 x 62 7/8 in. (116.5 x 159.5 cm)
